background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: I'm very impressed by everything you guys are saying and all the things that are happening, and I certainly agree with you. The one thing we're not saying is something I heard this morning from our Nobel Laureate panel was we're having trouble attracting people here because of the state of our education system. Now we're not talking about the higher education system.

background.speaker: [target]
background.text: which we all agree is fantastic, and we're doing great things in this state.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: But I'm worried because if it weren't for two southern states, when it comes to the health of our population, when it comes to the education of our population in general, we are at the bottom.

ground_truth: Let me challenge part of what you say, and let me tell you, I want to correct one factor in what you said, because I've lived this cycle, and we turn downward. Let me tell you the glass half full, and that is from 1983, when his father started working on K-12, to 2011. In 2011, this state led, not the southern states, but led the country in increase of academic achievement of the African American and Hispanic population, and the white population. Now, that came from a low base of about 48, but we moved up to 25th in the entire country in a relatively short period of time. In 2011, the state took $5 billion out of the K-12 education system funding, and decreased standards in 2011 by decreasing math and science requirements. So, beginning in 2011 to 2016, we began to decline again. That's one of the reasons that we started the state improvement effort, is because we believe we must rebuild the momentum that was created, really, by his father. But I think there is a growing awareness in the state that we took the foot off the pedal, and we, as I said earlier, we're in a race to see if we can turn around, again, our K-12 system, because if we don't, we're not going to be able to fill these jobs that are going to be needed in the future. So, I agree with part of what you said, but I don't think it's an impossible task, because we've done it once before. And it takes a long time. The education pipeline is long, but we've just expanded, for instance, early childhood education, made a major new investment in that. That's critical. But there's more to be done on the education front, trust me. If you looked at... If I looked at one summary of the issue the state faces over the next 20 years, it is we need a large, employable workforce. Large means we have to keep migration growing. Employable means we have to continue to improve the education system and health care outcomes. Right now, we have 1.2 million unfilled jobs in the state, and only 500,000 unemployed people. And those 500,000 do not qualify for the 1,200,000 unfilled jobs. So, yes, we have our challenges. But believe me, we're not behind like our competitor states are. And again, I wouldn't trade places with other states, given looking across the state. And part of what our state improvement initiative has done is measure our state against all the other 49 states, because we believe any enterprise must be looking at what are the strategic challenges you face down the road. And we face many challenges down the road, and a particular one is health care costs, health care outcomes, and we face a tremendous issue in terms of access to health care and affordability of health care.
